summary: An OCR-garbled 1945 Los Angeles Examiner account describes a man who met a friend at the Melody Lane Restaurant around July 28, 1915 (as stated in the text) and was later approached by an individual claiming knowledge of Hitler's escape. He claims Hitler and his party arrived by submarine on the Argentine coast near the Valdez peninsula in the Gulf of San Matias, were guided inland on horseback to a ranch in the Andes foothills, and that six Argentine officials helped. He was paid $15,000, wants immunity from being returned to Argentina, and offers directions to San Antonio, Argentina. Hitler is described as having asthma, ulcers, a shaved mustache, and a long scar on his upper lip. The text also notes that the story was given to the reporter on July 29, 1945, and that the writer contacted a Bureau of Investigation office in Los Angeles.

title: TheNazs are Winning in

nodes.title: TheNazs are Winning in (intro)
nodes.summary: A 1940s-era article on Nazi influence in Argentina. It describes a Council for Pan-American Democracy letter urging Truman to release a suppressed White Paper on the Peron regime. It names Nazi war criminals and agents (von Luxburg, Schroeder, Doenitz, Ley, Gestapo men) harbored in Argentina, their hidden funds, and hideouts in Cordoba, Entre Rios, Chaco and Misiones. It also covers Nazi economic ties involving Irigoyen, Peron, Fritz Mandl, GEOPE and Pistarini, plus reported continuing Nazi activity such as Labor Front deductions, a Nazi-geopolitics textbook, and clandestine airstrips.

Part two covers postwar Argentina: ex-ambassador Spruille Braden's critique of Axis spearheads, Peron's arrests of political prisoners, German economic penetration, and the Good Neighbor policy under Truman.

It covers doubts about the chauffeur's account of burning the bodies of Hitler and Eva Braun, the 92 charred bodies recovered from the bunker, dental and X-ray identification efforts, and sightings in Sweden, Argentina, Italy, Spain, and Japan. title: Hider Mystery Nazi Leaders
summary: A 1946 Central Press article by John F. Sembower on the unresolved fate of Adolf Hitler. Hitler's secretaries and a chauffeur claim he and Eva Braun died in the Berlin bunker, but no identifiable remains were found, feeding persistent sightings and rumors: a yacht off Sweden, a submarine landing in Argentina, Italy's Alto Adige, Spain, and a Japan-bound U-boat. Investigators check dental and X-ray records, and suspect Martin Bormann holds the key. Russian custody rumors are dismissed. The piece compares Hitler to legends like Lincoln's assassin John Wilkes Booth, Marshal Ney, and Attila the Hun, and notes a poll showing two-thirds of Americans believe he lives. It closes with FBI correspondence from J. Edgar Hoover on related tips.

title: Strike by Business Weapon Against Raise Ordered by Government
summary: A 1946-era United States News article reports a three-day strike by Argentine businessmen against a government decree, ordered by Col. Juan Peron's army-colonel government, raising wages 18 to 33 1/3 percent and paying a December bonus. Businesses refused on grounds of illegality (no Congress since 1943) and inability to pay, and took the decree to court. Peron, as Labor Minister, backed friendly unions and a profit-sharing decree, and his Labor Party nominated him for the February 24 presidential election. The article assesses his support from the Army, police, Catholic leaders, nationalists, and fascist sympathizers, versus opposition candidate Jose Tamborini's Democratic Union, and the swing groups of workers, estate owners, National Democrats, and apathetic citizens. It notes possible force and implications for U.S. relations.

A Pentagon-era office memo describes a brochure of originals with translations, signature comparisons requested by General Vandenberg to verify authenticity against captured Wehrmacht documents, and a request to keep the matter secret.

title: Office Memorandum

nodes.title: Office Memorandum (intro)
nodes.summary: A 1946 U.S. Government memorandum (March 6, 1946) from the FBI to Mr. Ladd transmits a brochure reproducing Adolf Hitler's marriage certificate, private will, and political testament, with German originals and English translations. It notes signatures of Hitler, Goebbels, Bormann, Burgdorf, and Krebs on these documents and on captured Wehrmacht papers. General Vandenberg asked the Bureau to compare signatures for authenticity, kept secret until verified. The FBI Laboratory report (March 13, 1946) finds the paper and handwriting consistent with genuineness, though the typed marriage form is questioned.

nodes.title: Daily Treatment of adolf
nodes.summary: A chronological diary-style medical log of Adolf Hitler's treatment from November 14 to December 30 (apparently 1944), kept by his physician. It records daily visits, appetite, sleep, and mood; injections (Trbz/Trebenerol-type solutions, Glyconorm, liver, Homoseran, vitamins); tonsil and throat treatments by Prof. von Eicken; a polyp operation; blood, urine, and stool tests; abdominal and gallbladder findings; jaundice signs; recurring tremors and spasms; and the attending doctors' visits and schedules. It ends with a March 1946 FBI memo certifying the authenticity of Hitler's private and political testament documents, which the Bureau's lab examined.

A man of 5'10-1/2" to 11" and 185 to 190 pounds, with no attempt at disguise, stayed at a hotel and played chess in the lobby after 11 p.m. with other visitors. nodes.summary: Describes a text about alleged sensational claims that Adolf Hitler survived in the savanna of Bogota, Colombia. It covers a letter from 'Amigo, amigo, amigo' demanding 50,000 dollars to reveal details, a submarine voyage, Eva Braun's death, and a supposed Hitler stay in Florida. It also covers a second letter from a purported Colombian, 'Isidoro Hame Seltz', who claims the story is true and links it to the assassination of Dr. Gaitan, which he calls a master coup against Communism.

nodes.title: May 19, 1948,
nodes.summary: A 1948 letter to the director of the newspaper RE Tiempo responds to a story about Hitler's presence in Bogota. The writer, a Colombian landowner educated in Europe, describes meeting Hitler at the 1926 Berlin Olympics, forming a friendship, and helping plan German-backed industrialization of Latin America. He says he was kept informed of Hitler's postwar plans since 1945, spent most of the war in Europe, and was persecuted by the Soviet GPU in late 1944 before escaping across a border.

nodes.title: January 12, 1945.— I received a visit from X, a well known German
nodes.summary: A first-person account, dated January 1945 onward, by a Colombian narrator recruited by a German agent (X) to find a South American hideout for Hitler and German scientists. The narrator recommends Colombia, specifically the unguarded Guajira coast and his family property in Nariño, and arranges a landing at Bahía Honda in July 1945 with contact men and a radio code based on Haydn's Toy Symphony. The narrator says Hitler changed plans, flew with Bormann, physicists, and secret documents in three Stinson planes that landed at La Florida near Bogotá, and then burned them. The group later operated from a Bogotá plantation, ran anti-Communist operations, and had a mole in the Soviet legation. The text then describes a plot to assassinate Jorge Eliécer Gaitán during the Ninth Pan American Conference to trigger a US-USSR war. Hitler vanished by April 15, and the author claims Eva Braun died of embolism during the submarine trip.

A 1948 Spanish-language newspaper article from El Tiempo (Bogota, Colombia), translated, with photostatic-copy notes. It covers claims that Adolf Hitler survived in Bogota: an anonymous letter demanding $50,000 for details (a submarine voyage, Eva Braun's death, a Florida stay); a second letter linking the story to Dr. Gaitan's assassination as an anti-Communist coup; a letter from a Colombian landowner who knew Hitler; and a first-person account of a plan to hide Hitler and German scientists in Colombia.

A 1948 translated letter from Mexico to the U.S. Investigation Department claims a young man (apparently Joachim von Ribbentrop) could reveal Hitler's hiding place for $20 million, denying he is in Spain or Argentina. Related garbled materials cover rumors Hitler lived in Bogota, Colombia: a Al Dia report of an Aruba letter, an FBI memo and Hoover letter, a Schacht clipping, and El Tiempo coverage of extortion letters, a coup theory linked to Gaitan's assassination, and a plan to hide Hitler and scientists in Colombia.

The author states he will not leave Berlin, the capital, and will choose death there when the Führer's seat can no longer be held. He cites refusing to surrender to enemies who would stage a spectacle for their masses, criticizes the unworthy conduct of some, and praises soldiers at the front, Berlin's women, farmers, workers, and youth.

title: Hitler's Political Testament: Final Call to Resist and Fight On
key_items: der deutschen Geschichte so oder einnal wieder
summary: A final message urging the defeat of Germany's enemies and continued struggle. It thanks the people and expresses gratitude and loyalty, linking the fight to Germany's history and the National Socialist movement's vision of a true people's community. It acknowledges soldiers' sacrifices and the author's personal bond with them, and reports that brave men and women chose to die with him, which he forbade in favor of continued national struggle. Leaders of the army, navy, and air force are ordered to strengthen soldiers' resistance in a National Socialist spirit, noting he himself chose death over capitulation.
